## Setting up a terminal

Below is a short overview per operating system. For step-by-step instructions with screenshots, see the [setup page of the Getting started with bash and an HPC tutorial](https://ndombrowski.github.io/cli_workshop/source/installation.html).

### Linux

Every Linux system comes with a terminal, and the shell is usually bash. Open the terminal from your applications menu, or search for "Terminal" (depending on your system it can also be called Konsole or xterm).

### Mac

Every Mac comes with a terminal. To open it, do one of these:

-   In Finder, go to **Go**, then **Utilities**, and open **Terminal**.
-   Or press Cmd + Space to open Spotlight, type `Terminal` and press Return.

Newer Macs (macOS Catalina and later) use zsh as their shell, not bash. Almost all commands on these pages work the same way in zsh. If you want to use bash, type `bash` in the terminal.

### Windows

Windows does not come with a terminal that understands bash commands, so you need to install one:

1.  **MobaXterm** (recommended if you are new to the command line): a small terminal program with the most common Linux commands built in. It can also connect to an HPC with SSH and transfer files with SCP/SFTP. See the [MobaXterm installation instructions](https://hpc.ncsu.edu/Documents/mobaxterm.php). The free Home Edition is all you need. The portable edition does not need administrator rights. By default, it deletes your files when you close it, so set a permanent home folder as described in the [tutorial setup page](https://ndombrowski.github.io/cli_workshop/source/installation.html).
2.  **Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2)**: installs a full Linux system (by default Ubuntu) inside Windows. This is a heavier installation that needs more disk space and memory, but it lets you use all Linux tools. See the [WSL installation instructions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install).

The code on these pages was run on a Windows machine using WSL2 and on a Linux machine.

### Check that your terminal works

After you set everything up and opened a terminal, you should see something like this:

<p align="center">
  <img width="500"  src="../../img/terminal.png">
</p>

Type the command below and press Enter:

```{bash}
# Print the name of the shell you are using
echo $SHELL
```

If the output ends with `bash` or `zsh` (e.g. `/bin/bash`), your terminal works.


### Putty/GIS study to connect to an HPC

If you don't need Bash on your computer and/or have trouble setting up a Bash terminal but want to analyze your data on an HPC that you already have access to, you can use the SSH-client [Putty](https://www.putty.org/) on the GIS studio computers. 

The [GIS-studio](https://amsuni.sharepoint.com/sites/GIS-Studio) was established in 2003 to serve staff and students of the Institute for Biodiversity and Ecosystem Dynamics (IBED) of the University of Amsterdam and to assist them in their spatial data analysis using Geographical Information Systems (GIS) and remote sensing (RS) software.  You can also use these computers to connect to an HPC.

More information on accessing the IBED Crunchomics HPC can be found [here](https://scienceparkstudygroup.github.io/software_information/source/cli/hpc_usage.html). 
If its your first time using bash and/or an HPC, it is recommended to look at this [mini-tutorial](https://ndombrowski.github.io/cli_workshop/).

To access to the GIS-studio computers:

1. Go to the [GIS-studio](https://amsuni.sharepoint.com/sites/GIS-Studio) website
2. Click on [ORS PC reservations](https://amsuni.sharepoint.com/sites/GIS-Studio/SitePages/ORS.aspx) 
3. Click on "ORS sheet 2024" and request access if you don't already have it 
4. After reserving a computer and starting it up find the Putty application
5. In the Host Name field, enter the hostname of the HPC you want to connect to. For example, for the UvA Crunchomics HPC, you would enter: UvanetID@omics-h0.science.uva.nl
6. Click "open"
7. Enter your UvanetID passport
8. You are now connected to the HPC
